newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's Zastava says car plant revival crucial.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's Zastava says car plant revival crucial.

text.p: Serbia's Zastava Group said on Wednesday a crucial revival programme at its car plant would help it to survive until it found a foreign partner.

"The revival programme for the car factory is 'to be or not to be' for the entire Group. It is an enormous task for all of us, but it simply must be carried out," Srboljub Vasovic, president of the Zastava Group, told Reuters.
"The programme will help us survive until we strike a deal with one of the world car producers," he said.

Zastava, which produces the small compact Yugo car, is looking to a potential foreign partner for financial help to develop and modernise production at its car plant. Zastava's latest model Yugo, Florida, was launched in 1988.
Vasovic said intensive negotiations were in progress with South Korea's Hyundai Motor Company, but refused to disclose the names of two companies he said were from Europe.
A source close to the Zastava's management said the talks were also in progress with Italy's Fiat SpA and France's PSA Peugeot Citroen.

The company, once the main industrial hard-currency earner for the former Yugoslavia, is sharing the destiny of the entire economy now struggling to find fresh funds to restart its operations after almost seven years of idleness.
The economy has been hard hit by the violent break-up of the ex-Yugoslav federation, war-related sanctions, loss of markets and mismanagement.

The Serbian government earlier this week said it would provide an initial financial injection of 70.2 million dinars ($12.3 million) for the plant's rehabilitation programme, which the company said was worth some 970 million dinars and would produce 22,250 cars by the year end.

Out of the total production, 10,000 cars are earmarked for sales abroad to Macedonia, Egypt, Jordan and Ecuador and the company said it expected to earn 10 million German marks ($5.8 million) in profits from the overseas sales.
Only some 2,000 cars were produced in the first three months of the year mainly due to lack of working capital, engines and other parts produced by local subcontractors who face similar problems.
Last year, despite the government help, the plant produced barely 10,000 cars compared to as many as 200,000 in 1990.
Vasovic admitted targeted output was at present extremely high but said it was a minimum to keep production going.
"We must start the production and increase capacity utilisation. This will boost our negotiating position and help us find an adequate partner," he said.
